subject: Accounting
title: Money Laundering Basics
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Money Laundering Basics.

hook.text: Drug money can't be deposited at a bank without questions. So criminals 'wash' it through legitimate businesses.

buildup.text: Money laundering has three stages: placement (get it in), layering (move it around), integration (use it).

discovery.text: Cash-intensive businesses like car washes and restaurants are classic laundering fronts—mixing dirty money with clean.

twist.text: Banks must file suspicious activity reports (SARs)—and forensic accountants analyze them for patterns.

climax.text: Global anti-money laundering rules require every financial institution to know their customers and flag anomalies.

punchline.text: Dirty money goes in. Clean-looking money comes out. Forensics spots the rinse.

quiz.question: What are the three stages of money laundering?

details.summary: Money laundering disguises the origins of illegally obtained money to make it appear legitimate. This topic covers the three stages—placement, layering, and integration—and how forensic accountants identify laundering patterns in financial records.
details.whyItMatters: Money laundering enables virtually all profit-driven crime. Without it, criminals can't use their proceeds. Forensic accountants who can identify laundering patterns can dismantle criminal enterprises.
takeaways: Placement introduces dirty money into the financial system through deposits, purchases, or businesses
Layering conceals the trail through complex transactions, shell companies, and international transfers
Integration returns the clean-looking money to the criminal through legitimate-appearing investments

faq.question: What are the three stages of money laundering?
faq.answer: Placement introduces illegal cash into the legitimate financial system. Layering disguises the trail through complex, often international transactions. Integration returns the now-clean-looking money to the launderer through legitimate investments, businesses, or purchases.

faq.question: How do forensic accountants detect money laundering?
faq.answer: They look for structuring (deposits just below reporting thresholds), unusual wire transfers, businesses with cash flows inconsistent with their industry, complex ownership structures with no business purpose, and transactions with high-risk jurisdictions.
